The syllabus covers core topics in single-variable calculus and basic linear algebra (derivatives, integration, matrices), but the pacing feels uneven and some topics are introduced quickly without enough time for consolidation.
​

The course is practical, but I sometimes felt the connection between calculus and linear algebra could be explained more clearly to help build intuition.
​
sections.teaching:
The instructor explains concepts clearly and is well-organized, and the lessons are easy to follow even when the material becomes challenging.
​

Good use of examples and step-by-step walkthroughs, and questions are handled patiently.
sections.grading:
Grading is generally fair and matches what is taught, and the assessment focuses on key skills like computation and applications.
​

Feedback could be a bit more detailed (especially on mistakes and how to improve), but overall the marking is reasonable.
sections.workload:
Workload is manageable for a 3-credit course, but it requires consistent weekly practice to keep up with the problem-solving.
​

If you stay on schedule with exercises and review regularly, it won’t be overwhelming.

sections.content:
3 parts:
Basic Financial Mathematics (very easy)
Linear Algebra
Calculus

For the midterm:
It covers Financial Mathematics and Linear Algebra. Calculators are allowed. The midterm is not very difficult—if you study the lecturer’s handwritten notes thoroughly, you should easily secure at least 80% (at least based on this year’s paper).

The sample paper has a similar difficulty level to the actual midterm. Some questions follow exactly the same format as those in the sample paper or the examples shown in lectures, with only the numbers changed. So make sure you understand and remember the steps for every type of question.

For those who have never studied linear algebra before: don’t worry, it’s perfectly manageable. It’s just basic mathematics that requires a bit more time to get used to. Personally, I didn’t take M1/M2 in HKDSE and only got Level 4 in Maths, yet I found the midterm very easy.

For the final:
Calculus only. No calculator is allowed, but you may bring one double-sided A4 cheat sheet.

This is where things get really challenging. Calculus is taught starting around Week 7, leaving only about 5-6 weeks to prepare for a final exam that is worth 65% of the total grade. Unlike the earlier topics, calculus involves a lot of symbolic manipulation—lots of variables, exponents, subscripts, integrals, derivatives, and complicated equations—rather than straightforward numerical calculations. Many new concepts are introduced, and they can be quite difficult for beginners to grasp.

This year, the final paper was WAY MORE HARDER than the sample paper, so don’t be misled into thinking that memorising the solutions from the sample will be enough. It absolutely won’t.

The exam was genuinely tough—you’ll see what I mean when you look at the grade statistics below. To do well, you need to practise more difficult exercises from the textbook. The TA exercises, lecture examples, and sample paper are far too easy to prepare you adequately. Make sure you’re thoroughly prepared!

sections.content:
The course content is a well-structured survey of essential mathematical tools for business and social sciences. It is highly practical and application-oriented.

Part 1: Finance & Algebra (Ch. 3 & 4): The course starts with the mathematics of finance (simple/compound interest, annuities, amortization), which is immediately relevant for any business student. This is followed by an extensive unit on matrices and systems of linear equations. This section is fundamental for understanding data organization, solving multi-variable problems, and is a building block for more advanced topics like operations research.

Part 2: Differential Calculus (Ch. 10, 11, 12): This is the core of the course. It covers limits, the derivative, and all its applications. Key topics include various rules of differentiation (product, quotient, chain), implicit differentiation, and concepts like elasticity of demand. The most valuable part is applying derivatives to curve sketching and optimization (finding max profit, min cost), which are crucial for economic modeling and decision-making.

Part 3: Integral Calculus (Ch. 13 & 14): The course concludes with integration, covering antiderivatives, the fundamental theorem of calculus, and techniques like substitution. The applications to area between curves and analyzing probability density functions provide a strong foundation for economic analysis and statistics.

Overall: The content is demanding but incredibly useful. It doesn't delve into the deep theoretical proofs of higher-level calculus but focuses intensely on how to use these tools, which is exactly what a business student needs.

The course mainly covers four sections: Matrices, Financial Mathematics, Differentiation and Integration. The Mid-term Exam covers the former two topics; where Finals covers the latter two topics excluding any syllabus covered in the Mid-term examination.
The content is pretty easy for newbies in calculus and statistics: The financial maths covers a couple of formulas that are not too complicated. However, all the content requires a lot of practices to master the steps and treatments for different question types.

sections.content: This course teaches basic calculus.  Professor Li plan the time well.  All the materials are covered in a suitable speed.  Answer students' questions in a very detailed way.  Sometimes I think it is too detail and uses too much time.  But I admit that every student has different ability so I really appreciate his patience and willingness to teach.
sections.teaching: Professor Li is a wonderful professor.  Willing to spend his spare time after lessons answering questions, replies email quickly, gives a lot of reminders before mid-term and final exam.  Maths really requires students to do a lot of practice.  Professor Li mentioned this again and again.  He also provided us some recommended questions.  Those questions save our time finding suitable practice.  2 past papers are provided before mid term and final respectively.  Overall a wonderful professor.
sections.grading: The grade of this course is curved within ALL classes according to Professor Li.  So that means no matter you are taught by which professor, your grade will not be affected.  I got over 90% in both mid term and final, final grade is A+.  So just work hard and do more practice.  Which class you are in will not affect your grade much since it is curved within ALL classes.
sections.workload: Just some basic online homework.  Plenty of time for you to do it.  Moreover, no limit in answering the questions.  That means you can try it again and again until you get the correct answer.  You can also ask your friends to do the homework for you (not recommended but you can do so if you are running out of time).  Overall very small workload to me

sections.content:
The course covers mathematics for finance (some concepts like present value, future value and annuity etc.), matrix, differentiation and integration. As most of the students taking this course are business students, the syllabus also covers some applications of the mathematical concepts, like two-industries models and marginal analysis in economics. The content in this course can hence be applied in other business core courses, for example, I found the mathematics for finance particularly useful in accounting course, which covers the computation of bonds' present value.

Although some examples covered in differentiation and integration require the use of calculators, Mid-term 2 (just testing differentiation) and Final Exam (testing differentiation and integration) mainly examine your ability to apply the concepts taught. Those questions do not appear in these exams, hence no calculators are allowed.
sections.teaching:
Prof. Li will do some proof and steps on the white board for some difficult mathematical concepts and examples in class, so that we can have more thorough understanding about the content. However, he is not always able to make verbal explanations of the concepts clearly. If you have no idea about what he is talking about, referring to the white board might be a good choice for you.

TA is Kitty. She makes her own tutorial notes, including some crucial formulas and concepts for each topic, followed by a lot of exercises. The tutorial notes are pretty useful and she will put the solution of the exercises on her own webpage. She will also go through some questions to clear our misunderstandings. In spite of her low voice which makes the tutorials a bit boring, I still think that attending the tutorials is beneficial to you.
